newsitem.title: USA: Panel says U.S. inflation overstated by 1.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: Panel says U.S. inflation overstated by 1.1 pct.

text.p: A congressionally appointed commission estimated on Wednesday that government statistics overstate inflation by 1.1 percentage points a year, a finding with major implications for the federal budget and the whole U.S. economy.

The panel recommended action by the Clinton administration and Congress to fix the problem, including potential legislation to alter the way tax brackets and costly programmes like Social Security are adjusted for cost-of-living changes.

"They should first make a decision about whether what they are really trying to do is accurately, fully and fairly insulate people from inflation," said Michael Boskin, a Stanford University economist who led the five-member group.
"If that is their purpose, no more and no less, then they need to change what they do," he added.

Quoting Congressional Budget Office estimates, the commission said the upward bias in the Consumer Price Index as now compiled would add $148 billion to the federal budget deficit by 2006 if not fixed.
In the shorter run, a revised index would lower estimates of the federal budget deficit, possibly making it easier for Democrats and Republicans to agree on balancing the budget.
Although the potential savings are huge, the political difficulties were apparent as influential groups were quick to express concern.
Horace Deets, executive director of the American Association of Retired Persons, took aim at the idea of using legislation to change the CPI.

"To decrease the CPI arbitrarily through legislation means that the income of virtually anyone who pays taxes, receives Social Security benefits, veteran benefits or federal pensions would be stripped away by inflation," he said in a statement.
AFL-CIO President John Sweeney said the Boskin group's views should be taken seriously but they should not be the last word. He also echoed concern for impact on the elderly.
Some economists, however, praised the report, saying its suggestions would correct what has been in effect an overpayment for programmes like Social Security.

"We told (senior citizens) that we were going to maintain their standard of living," said economist Roger Brinner of DRI/McGraw-Hill. "Instead we've been exaggerating the increase in standard of living."

Social Security recipients who receive average monthly checks of $745 would get $8 less of an increase in their cost-of-living if the CPI were adjusted to account for the panel's estimated bias. The impact would accumulate, though, meaning a reduction of almost $100 five years from now.
Also, some taxpayers whose incomes are rising would pay more, as a lower CPI would mean they would hit higher tax brackets more quickly.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, said any CPI reform would require bipartisan effort, including leadership from President Bill Clinton.
"I want to stress that any action we take on this report must be broadly and deeply bipartisan," Roth said. "We must also have the full cooperation and leadership by the Clinton administration."
Roth urged quick action on the report and said he intended to hold hearings on the commission report early next year.
In a careful response, White House economic adviser Joseph Stiglitz said the Clinton administration would study the report as well as other views on measuring the cost of living.

"The Clinton administration believes that it is important to have the most accurate measure possible to ensure that Social Security and other benefits are protected from inflation and to adjust tax brackets to keep our tax system fair," Stiglitz said in a statement.

The report highlighted several reasons for the upward bias to the CPI, including the difficulty in capturing the effects of changes in consumers' spending patterns and the impact of the introduction of new products.

Boskin, a former economic adviser to President George Bush who was named to head the panel last year by the Senate Finance Committee, said much of the CPI overstatement could be fixed but it would take a while.
"We are all going to need some time," he told reporters.
